topics.title: The Shortest Distance Between a Plane and a Point

fields.value: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(5,9,-6)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $3x+2y+7z=-9.$

Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=2$ and $y=3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+7z & =-9 \\ 3(2)+2(3)+7z & =-9 \\ 7z & =-21 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(2,3,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,-3⟩-⟨5,9,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-6,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨3,2,7⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-3)\cdot 3+(-6)\cdot 2+3\cdot 7|}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{7}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-9-12+21|}{\sqrt{9+4+49}} \\  & =\frac{|\,0\,|}{\sqrt{62}} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $P$ lies on the plane.

fields.value: Given the Cartesian equation $x-y+4z+16=0$ of the plane $\mathrm{Π}$, find an equation of $\mathrm{Π}$ in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p})\cdot \mathbf{n}=0.$

First, from the equation of the plane we get that the normal vector of $\mathrm{Π}$ is $\mathbf{n}=⟨1,-1,4⟩.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $\mathrm{Π}$ for $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+4z+16 & =0 \\ z & =-\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}y-4.\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $x=0$ and $y=0$, we get $z=-4.$ Hence, the point $P(0,0,-4)$ lies on $\mathrm{Π}.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=⟨0,0,-4⟩.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p})\cdot \mathbf{n} & =0 \\ (\mathbf{r}-⟨0,0,-4⟩)\cdot ⟨1,-1,4⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,-1,4)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,-1,4⟩-⟨2,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨3,-6,-6⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$

Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\mathrm{Π}:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c},$ $t,s\in \mathbb{R}$, where  $\mathbf{b}=⟨1,5,8⟩$, $\mathbf{c}=⟨-1,-1,-3⟩$, and  $\mathbf{u}=⟨-3,5,-7⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}.$

By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 5 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-t=-3 \\ 5s-t=5 \\ 8s-3t=-7\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & 5 \\ 8 & -3 & -7\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ 8 & -3 & -7\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-8{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 20 \\ 0 & 5 & 17\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 17\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=-8,$ which has no solution.

So, there are no values of $s$ and $t$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc=u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $u$ does *not* lie on the plane $Π.$

fields.value: Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\mathrm{Π}:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, $t,s\in \mathbb{R}$, where  $\mathbf{b}=⟨-1,3,5⟩$, $\mathbf{c}=⟨1,-5,-7⟩$, and  $\mathbf{u}=⟨1,-8,-10⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}.$

By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathrm{Π}$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c} & =\mathbf{u} \\ s\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -5 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -8 \\ -10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+t &=1 \\ 3s-5t &=-8 \\ 5s-7t &=-10\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 \\ 5 & -7 & -10\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 \\ 5 & -7 & -10\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & -2 & -5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+t &=1 \\ -2t &=-5 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
-2t=-5\,⟹\,t=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+t & =1 \\ -s+\frac{5}{2} & =1 \\ -s & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ s & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=\frac{3}{2},\,t=\frac{5}{2},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{b}+\frac{5}{2}\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $$
\displaystyle s\cdot t=\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{5}{2}=\frac{15}{4}.
$$

fields.value: Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\mathrm{Π}:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c},$ $t,s\in \mathbb{R}$, where  $\mathbf{b}=⟨-1,3,2⟩$, $\mathbf{c}=⟨2,-1,-1⟩$, and  $\mathbf{u}=⟨5,-5,-4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}.$

By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathrm{Π}$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c} & =\mathbf{u} \\ s\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -5 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+2t &=5 \\ 3s-t &=-5 \\ 2s-t &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 & -5 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+2t &=5 \\ t &=2 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+2t & =5 \\ -s+2(2) & =5 \\ -s+4 & =5 \\ s & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-1,\,t=2,$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=-\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-1)\cdot 2=-2.$

fields.value: Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\mathrm{Π}:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c},$ $t,s\in \mathbb{R}$, where  $\mathbf{b}=⟨1,-2,-1⟩$, $\mathbf{c}=⟨-4,5,-1⟩$, and  $\mathbf{u}=⟨1,1,4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}.$

By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathrm{Π}$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c} & =\mathbf{u} \\ s\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-4t &=1 \\ -2s+5t &=1 \\ -s-t &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -4 & 1 \\ -2 & 5 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 3 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -5 & 5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-4t &=1 \\ t &=-1 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-1.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-4t & =1 \\ s-4(-1) & =1 \\ s+4 & =1 \\ s & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-3,\,t=-1,$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=-3\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-3)\cdot (-1)=3.$

\left\{\begin{aligned}-s-3t &=5 \\ -s-8t &=-10 \\ 4s+14t &=-14\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ -1 & -8 & -10 \\ 4 & 14 & -14\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -15 \\ 4 & 14 & -14\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -15 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s-3t &=5 \\ t &=3 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=3.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s-3t & =5 \\ -s-3(3) & =5 \\ -s-9 & =5 \\ s & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-14,\,t=3,$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=-14\mathbf{b}+3\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-14)\cdot 3=-42.$

fields.value: Given the Cartesian equation $4x+4y-2z=0$ of the plane $\mathrm{Π}$, find an equation of $\mathrm{Π}$ in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p})\cdot \mathbf{n}=0.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $\mathrm{Π}$ for $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+4y-2z & =0 \\ 2z & =4x+4y \\ z & =2x+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p})\cdot \mathbf{n} & =0 \\ (\mathbf{r}-⟨0,0,0⟩)\cdot ⟨4,4,-2⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(1,-2,1).$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, from the equation of the plane, we get a normal vector $n=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|0\cdot (-2)+(-4)\cdot 1+4\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4+8|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}} \\  & =\frac{|4|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-24,8,6⟩ & =⟨-12,10,6⟩\cdot ⟨-24,8,6⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-24,8,6⟩ & =404.\end{aligned}

Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\mathrm{Π}:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c},$ $t,s\in \mathbb{R}$, where  $\mathbf{b}=⟨1,7,-3⟩$, $\mathbf{c}=⟨-8,10,-4⟩$, and  $\mathbf{u}=⟨6,9,-4⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}.$

By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathrm{Π}$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c} & =\mathbf{u} \\ s\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 7 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ 10 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 9 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-8t &=6 \\ 7s+10t &=9 \\ -3s-4t &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 7 & 10 & 9 \\ -3 & -4 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-7{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 66 & -33 \\ -3 & -4 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 66 & -33 \\ 0 & -28 & 14\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{66}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & -28 & 14\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+28{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -8 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-8t &=6 \\ t &=-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-8t & =6 \\ s-8\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) & =6 \\ s+4 & =6 \\ s & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=2,\,t=-\frac{1}{2},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=2\mathbf{b}-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-1.$

Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\mathrm{Π}:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, $t,s\in \mathbb{R}$, where  $\mathbf{b}=⟨-1,2,3⟩$, $\mathbf{c}=⟨3,-7,-9⟩$, and  $\mathbf{u}=⟨2,-3,-6⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}.$

By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathrm{Π}$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c} & =\mathbf{u} \\ s\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -7 \\ -9\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+3t &=2 \\ 2s-7t &=-3 \\ 3s-9t &=-6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -7 & -3 \\ 3 & -9 & -6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 3 & -9 & -6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+3t &=2 \\ -t &=1 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
-t=1\,⟹\,t=-1.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+3t & =2 \\ -s+3(-1) & =2 \\ -s & =5 \\ s & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-5,\,t=-1,$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=-5\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-5)\cdot (-1)=5.$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+t &=1 \\ 4s-6t &=-10 \\ 3s-7t &=-15\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-s+t &=1 \\ -2t &=-6 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
-2t=-6\,⟹\,t=3.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+t & =1 \\ -s+3 & =1 \\ -s & =-2 \\ s & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=2,\,t=3,$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=2\mathbf{b}+3\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=2\cdot 3=6.$

By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathrm{Π}$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c} & =\mathbf{u} \\ s\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 7 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -10 \\ 12\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 11 \\ -12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-2t &=2 \\ 7s-10t &=11 \\ -6s+12t &=-12\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 7 & -10 & 11 \\ -6 & 12 & -12\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-7{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & -3 \\ -6 & 12 & -12\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s-2t &=2 \\ 4t &=-3 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
4t=-3\,⟹\,t=-\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s-2t & =2 \\ s-2\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) & =2 \\ s+\frac{3}{2} & =2 \\ s & =2-\frac{3}{2} \\ s & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=\frac{1}{2},\,t=-\frac{3}{4},$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}-\frac{3}{4}\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $$
\displaystyle s\cdot t=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)=-\frac{3}{8}.
$$

topics.title: The Shortest Distance Between a Plane and a Point

fields.value: Given that $Q(1,3,4)$ lies on the plane $Π:r\cdot ⟨-4,2,0⟩=2$, find the shortest distance from $P(5,-2,3)$ to $Π.$

First, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,3,4⟩-⟨5,-2,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,5,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-4,2,0⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-4)\cdot (-4)+5\cdot 2+1\cdot 0|}{\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|16+10+0|}{\sqrt{16+4+0}} \\  & =\frac{|26|}{\sqrt{20}} \\  & =\frac{13\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

fields.value: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2,11,1)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $r\cdot ⟨2,-5,4⟩=20.$

First, we need to find a point on the plane. If $r=⟨x,y,z⟩,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨2,-5,4⟩ & =20 \\ 2x-5y+4z & =20 \\ 4z & =20-2x+5y \\ z & =5-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $x=2$ and $y=4,$ we get 

$$
z=5-\frac{1}{2}(2)+\frac{5}{4}(4)=9.
$$

So, the point $Q(2,4,9)$ lies on the plane. 

Now, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,4,9⟩-⟨-2,11,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-7,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $n=⟨2,-5,4⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(4)\cdot 2+(-7)\cdot (-5)+8\cdot 4|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-5)^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|8+35+32|}{\sqrt{4+25+16}} \\  & =\frac{|75|}{\sqrt{45}} \\  & =5\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-3y+6z & =-18 \\ 6(1)-3(2)+6z & =-18 \\ 6z & =-18 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,2,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,2,-3⟩-⟨5,4,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨6,-3,6⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-4)\cdot 6+(-2)\cdot (-3)+1\cdot 6|}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{6}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-24+6+6|}{\sqrt{36+9+36}} \\  & =\frac{|\,-12\,|}{\sqrt{81}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}

fields.value: Given the Cartesian equation $3x+5y+15=0$ of the plane $\mathrm{Π}$, find an equation of $\mathrm{Π}$ in the form $(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p})\cdot \mathbf{n}=0.$

First, from the equation of the plane we get that the normal vector of $\mathrm{Π}$ is $\mathbf{n}=⟨3,5,0⟩.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $\mathrm{Π}$ for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+5y+15 & =0 \\ 5y & =-3x-15 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{5}x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $x=0$, we get $y=-3.$ Hence, the point $P(0,-3,0)$ lies on $\mathrm{Π}.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $\mathbf{p}=⟨0,-3,0⟩.$

fields.value: Determine if the vector $\mathbf{u}$ lies on the plane $\mathrm{Π}:\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}$, $t,s\in \mathbb{R}$, where  $\mathbf{b}=⟨1,2,3⟩$, $\mathbf{c}=⟨3,8,-7⟩$, and  $\mathbf{u}=⟨9,22,-5⟩.$ In the affirmative case, find the value of $s\cdot t$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{u}=s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c}.$

By definition, $\mathbf{u}\in \mathrm{Π}$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}s\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{c} & =\mathbf{u} \\ s\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 8 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 22 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s+3t &=9 \\ 2s+8t &=22 \\ 3s-7t &=-5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 2 & 8 & 22 \\ 3 & -7 & -5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 3 & -7 & -5\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -16 & -32\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+8{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}s+3t &=9 \\ 2t &=4 \\ 0 &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
2t=4\,⟹\,t=2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s+3t & =9 \\ s+3(2) & =9 \\ s & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=3,\,t=2,$ we conclude that $\mathbf{u}$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
\mathbf{u}=3\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{c}.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=3\cdot 2=6.$
$u$ does not lie on $Π$

$$

From the equation of a plane in the parametric form $r=p+tv+sw$, we have that its normal vector is $n=v\times w.$ In our case, the normal vector to $Π$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =v\times w \\  & =⟨4,3,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,5⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 4 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 2 & 5\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =15i-20j+8k \\  & =⟨15,-20,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane $Π$ in dot product form is

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ & =⟨10,-5,12⟩\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨15,-20,8⟩ & =346.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

To compute the angle between the planes, we compute the angle between the corresponding normal vectors.

- The equation of the plane ${Π}_{1}$ is given in the form $(r-p)\cdot n=0,$ so the normal vector is ${n}_{1}=⟨2,1,-1⟩.$

- From the equation of a plane in the Cartesian form $ax+by+cz=d,$ we have a normal vector to the plane given by $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ In our case, then, the normal vector to ${Π}_{2}$ is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,2,1⟩.$

Now, we compute the angle between ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{{n}_{1}\cdot {n}_{2}}{|{n}_{1}||{n}_{2}|} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+1\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{3}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the principal value, we get 

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arccos}⁡\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)={60}^{∘}.
$$
